item.title: MetalMatters: The Best Metal Albums of February 2026
item.description: In February's best metal, Worm go from underground to mainstream, Incandescence unleash blackened Quebecois bliss, and Gorrch offer dissonance and immediacy.

item.title: Kerrin Connolly Swings for the Fences on Brilliant LP
item.description: Kerrin Connolly has stepped up her game, with smart, sophisticated arrangements and an arsenal of pop songs that are a quantum leap from earlier music.

item.title: Hilary Duff Grows Up on ‘Luck… or Something’
item.description: Hilary Duff toes the line between acoustic and dance-pop, but she ties it all together with songwriting about, for lack of a better term, millennial ennui.

item.title: The Avett Brothers’ Bob Crawford on His “Song” for John Quincy Adams
item.description: Quiet moments on the road with the Avett Brothers became Bob Crawford's research time to write his own sort of "song" for John Quincy Adams.

item.title: Shinedown’s ‘Rock the Country’ Controversy Proves Nothing Is Safe from Politics
item.description: Years of kindness and calls for unity from a band like Shinedown, whose very name implies radiant light, warrant a thoughtful, rather than reactive, pause.

item.title: The Setting Create a Unique Twist on the Jazz Trio
item.description: Jazz trio the Setting have brought to fruition Eivind Opsvik's love of 1970s and 1980s synthesizer music, ECM solo guitar albums, and experimental art pop.

item.title: Felsmann + Tiley Explore The Absurdity of Human Existence
item.description: Over crafted, textured synths, palpitating rhythms and intricate soundscapes, Felsmann + Tiley's music sounds jaw-droppingly expansive.

item.title: Converge Retake Their Ground on New Record
item.description: If Love Is Not Enough announces anything, it's a return to the stark architecture and the blunt-force grammar Converge helped codify.

item.title: Massive Attack’s ‘Blue Lines’ Changed Everything
item.description: Massive Attack provided the first truly viable British response to the then-rising—and stubbornly indigenous—sensibilities of American hip-hop culture.

item.title: 10 Writers Remaking African Literature in 2026
item.description: The writers demanding our attention in 2026 interrogate power, dissect masculinity, and insist on joy in their works of satire, sorcery, and secrets from Africa and the Diaspora.
